title: Employee Turnover in Malaysia: Causes, Industry Data and How to Reduce It (2027)
summary: Malaysia's employee turnover rate is 18.2%. Learn why people leave, which industries are hit hardest, and how HR can reduce attrition in 2027
body_markdown:
**The short answer:** Malaysia's employee attrition rate was 18.2% in 2025, among the three highest in Southeast Asia, according to[Aon](https://asianews.network/?p=245365) . Employees mostly leave over work-life balance, limited career growth and poor managers, not pay alone. Companies that cut turnover listen continuously, fix the first 90 days, equip their managers and act on early warning signs before resignations land.


Malaysian HR leaders are heading into 2027 with a familiar problem and fewer ways to solve it. Businesses are budgeting an average salary increase of 4.8% for 2026 ([Aon](https://www.aon.com/apac/in-the-press/asia-newsroom/2025/aon-survey-projects-4-8-percent-salary-growth-for-malaysia-in-2026) ), so buying loyalty with pay is not on the table. Meanwhile, 62% of Malaysian employees say now is a good time to find a job where they live ([Gallup](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/706178/state-global-workplace-malaysia-country-level-data.aspx) ).


If you cannot outbid the market, you have to out-listen it. This guide covers what the numbers say, why people leave, which industries feel it most, and what works.


### What is the employee turnover rate in Malaysia?


Aon's 2025 Salary Increase and Turnover Study surveyed more than 700 businesses across six Southeast Asian countries. Malaysia's attrition rate came in at 18.2%, behind only the Philippines and Singapore ([Aon](https://asianews.network/?p=245365) ).

Put simply, a Malaysian company with 1,000 employees replaces about 180 people a year. In retail and hospitality, it is closer to 220.


### Why do employees leave companies in Malaysia?


Pay matters, but it is rarely the whole story. Randstad's 2026 Employer Brand Research found that reliable pay and benefits are the top driver of job security, cited by 66% of Malaysian talent. Yet the most common reasons people actually leave are different ([Randstad](https://www.randstad.com.my/hr-trends/employer-brand/employee-retention-workplace-stability-malaysia/) ):


- **Work-life balance:** 41% leave because of a lack of it.
- **Career growth:** 40% leave because of limited progression.


Two further patterns stand out in Malaysian data.


**Bad managers and toxic teams drive people out.** In Randstad's 2025 Workmonitor, 59% of Malaysian employees said they had resigned because of a toxic workplace, the highest share in Asia Pacific ([SAYS](https://pre.says.com/my/lifestyle/59-of-malaysians-quit-jobs-due-to-toxic-managers-the-highest-in-asia-pacific) ). Randstad has also found that half of Malaysian workers would consider resigning over a poor relationship with their manager ([DataOn, citing Randstad](https://dataon.com/en-my/blog/why-employees-resign/) ).


**Burnout is common.** The Jobstreet by SEEK Workplace Happiness Index 2026 found that 41% of Malaysian workers feel burnt out, and only 36% are happy with their stress levels ([DataOn, citing Jobstreet](https://dataon.com/en-my/blog/why-employees-resign/) ).


Underneath all of this sits an engagement gap. Only 25% of Malaysian employees are engaged at work, in line with the Southeast Asian average ([Gallup](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/706178/state-global-workplace-malaysia-country-level-data.aspx) ). The other three in four are doing the job without much attachment to it, and they are the ones who leave when a better offer comes along.


### Which industries in Malaysia face the biggest retention problems?


#### Retail, hospitality and frontline-heavy sectors


Retail and hospitality have the highest attrition in Malaysia at 22.2% ([Aon](https://asianews.network/?p=245365) ). Most of these employees never sit at a desk or open a work email. That makes them hard to hear through annual surveys and intranet announcements, which are built for office staff.


#### Shared services and global business services


Malaysia is one of Asia's most mature shared services hubs, and 86% of Malaysia-based centres deliver several functions across multiple countries ([SSON](https://www.ssonetwork.com/events-ssomalaysia/downloads/state-of-industry-report-2026-shared-services-remain-a-cornerstone-of-enterprise-operations) ). Three pressures make retention harder here:


- **The first 90 days.** Daythree, a Malaysian business process outsourcing firm, calls the first 90 days the most critical retention period. It points to gaps between what new hires expect and what the job involves, and to unclear roles. Industry-wide early-attrition data is weakly tracked ([SAYS](https://says.com/my/news/malaysia-job-losses-early-attrition-90-days-service-sector-2026) ).
- **AI uncertainty.** A government-commissioned study found that 24% of global business services roles in Malaysia are highly affected by AI and 65% are moderately affected ([Bernama](https://bernama.com/en/thoughts/news.php?id=2578155) ). In our view, people who think their role is shrinking start looking before anyone tells them to.
- **More contract roles.** Randstad notes that contract roles are now a strategic choice in project-driven sectors such as shared services ([Focus Malaysia](https://focusmalaysia.my/?p=229817) ). Contract staff are harder to engage and easier to lose.


#### Banking and financial services


Banking is more stable than most Malaysian sectors ([People Matters](https://sea.peoplemattersglobal.com/amp/article/economy-policy/malaysias-talent-paradox-as-companies-seek-workers-employees-look-elsewhere-46315) ). The problem is narrower and more expensive. Shortages are concentrated in risk, compliance and digitally enabled finance roles ([BTI Executive Search and PERSOL](https://cdn-01.cms-ap-v2i.applyflow.com/bti-executives/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/BTI-Executive-Search_Industry-Insight-Report_2026.pdf) ). Losing one experienced risk analyst can hurt more than losing ten branch staff, because the replacement may take months to find.


#### Manufacturing and technology


Manufacturing attrition is 17.7% and technology is 17.1% ([Aon](https://asianews.network/?p=245365) ). At the same time, 24,100 Malaysian workers were retrenched in the first quarter of 2026 ([SAYS, citing SOCSO](https://says.com/my/news/malaysia-job-losses-early-attrition-90-days-service-sector-2026) ). Layoffs create a different retention risk: the people who remain may stay but disengage. Monroe Consulting argues that in Malaysia's 2026 workforce, quiet quitting is becoming more common than outright resignation ([Monroe](https://www.monroeconsulting.com/blog/2026/03/retention-in-malaysia-2026-why-disengagement-is-the-real-risk) ).


### What does employee turnover really cost?


Most companies only count the recruiter fee. The full cost includes:


- **Hiring:** job adverts, agency fees and interview time.
- **Ramp-up:** weeks or months before the new hire is fully productive.
- **Lost knowledge:** client relationships, process know-how and context that leave with the person.
- **Team strain:** colleagues covering the gap, which feeds the burnout that caused the exit.
- **Manager time:** every exit pulls a manager away from running the team.


Add those up for 180 exits a year and turnover becomes a board-level number, not an HR metric.


### How can Malaysian companies reduce employee attrition?


1. **Listen continuously, not once a year.** An annual survey tells you why people were unhappy after many of them have already left. Short, regular check-ins at key moments catch problems while you can still fix them.
2. **Fix the first 90 days.** Check in at day 7, 30, 60 and 90. Ask whether the job matches what was promised. Daythree reports lower attrition in the first six months after it added structured check-ins and clearer role expectations ([SAYS](https://says.com/my/news/malaysia-job-losses-early-attrition-90-days-service-sector-2026) ).
3. **Make managers the retention strategy.** Gallup finds that 70% of the variance in team engagement comes down to the manager ([Vulcan Post, citing Gallup](https://vulcanpost.com/?p=912012) ). Give managers team-level insight and simple actions, not a 60-page report.
4. **Show people where they can go next.** With 40% leaving over limited career growth, visible internal moves matter. In shared services, where roles are standardised, a clear path from processing to analysis to leadership is a retention tool.
5. **Treat work-life balance as a workload problem.** Flexible hours help, but if the workload stays the same, burnout follows. Watch for teams with high overtime and falling sentiment.
6. **Look for silent employees.** The people who stop answering surveys and stop speaking up are often the next to leave. Silence is a signal, not an absence of problems.
7. **Free HR business partners to do people work.** In large shared services and frontline workforces, HR teams lose hours to routine questions about leave, payslips and policies. Automating those gives HRBPs time for the conversations that keep people.
8. **Listen in the language people use.** Malaysian workforces mix Malay, English, Mandarin and Tamil. Feedback in a second language is shorter, safer and less honest.


### What to look for in an employee experience platform


If you are choosing an employee experience platform to support retention, check for these capabilities:


- **Lifecycle listening:** check-ins from onboarding through to exit, not just an annual survey.
- **Early warning:** flags employees at risk of leaving, with the reason, while there is time to act.
- **Channels employees already use:** Microsoft Teams, Slack, mobile and, for frontline staff, messaging apps.
- **Local languages:** Malay, Mandarin and Tamil as well as English.
- **Manager-ready insight:** clear actions for each team, not raw data.
- **HR query automation:** answers routine questions so HR has time for retention work.
- **Security:** certifications such as ISO 27001 and SOC 2.


### How Amber helps Malaysian companies reduce turnover


Amber is inFeedo's AI HRBP. She checks in with employees at the moments that matter across the lifecycle, from onboarding to exit, and achieves a 90% survey response rate ([inFeedo](https://www.infeedo.ai/listening) ). Her People to Meet algorithm predicts turnover risk and flags silent employees, who inFeedo's data shows are three times more likely to quit.


The results are clearest in captive centres that look like Malaysia's shared services hubs. At Sony India Software Center, attrition fell from 12.5% to about 8% over two years, and 83% of at-risk employees flagged by Amber were retained ([inFeedo](https://infeedo.ai/customers/sony-india-saved-hr-time-reduced-attrition) ). At Genpact, Amber talks to 130,000 employees, and those who engage with her are twice as likely to stay ([inFeedo](https://www.infeedo.ai/) ). ### FAQ


**What is the average employee turnover rate in Malaysia?** Malaysia's attrition rate was 18.2% in 2025, according to Aon's Salary Increase and Turnover Study, among the three highest in Southeast Asia.


**Which industry has the highest employee turnover in Malaysia?** Retail and hospitality, at 22.2% in 2025, followed by manufacturing at 17.7% and technology at 17.1%.


**Why do employees resign in Malaysia?** The most common reasons are poor work-life balance (41%) and limited career growth (40%), according to Randstad's 2026 research. Toxic workplaces and poor managers are also major drivers.


**Is employee turnover higher in Malaysia or Singapore?** Singapore's 2025 attrition rate was slightly higher at 19.3%, compared with 18.2% in Malaysia.


**How can HR predict which employees will leave?** Look for falling sentiment, silence in surveys, early-tenure doubts and manager friction. Continuous listening platforms combine these signals to flag employees at risk before they resign.
